source_read: Publisher HTML (JAMA Network, JAMA Psychiatry 2013;70(3):319-324), opened on the second attempt after a Cloudflare check cleared without interaction: structured abstract, introduction, Method (participants and procedure, measures, design and analysis), Results (sample characteristics, relationship between psychotic symptoms and methamphetamine use, the Table in full, predicted probabilities, further adjustment for health and social functioning), and the Comment up to the paragraph on symptoms during abstinence. The remainder of the Comment (limitations), the Figure (image) and the article information (funding, conflicts) could not be read because the browser device disconnected (see report).

claims.overstatement: Minor. (1) 'Roughly halved the odds ratios (2.25 and 3.90)': 4.0 to 2.25 is a 44% reduction, but 11.2 to 3.90 is a 65% reduction (about a third of the model-2 OR); 'roughly halved' fits only on the log-odds scale (56-58% of the log-OR retained). Suggested: 'reduced them to 2.25 and 3.90'. (2) The predicted 7% and 48% are for months with fewer than 16 days of cannabis and alcohol use; with frequent cannabis and/or alcohol use the predicted probability rose to 61-69%. (3) The further-adjusted model includes concurrent unemployment, housing, income, distress and disability, which may be consequences of use or of psychosis (mediators) as well as confounders, so it is not simply 'better adjusted'.
claims.note: All numbers reproduce: 278 analysed (501 MATES participants minus 17 not dependent, 59 with lifetime schizophrenia or mania, 138 without diagnostic data, 9 with no use in any observed month); 4 one-month windows (baseline, 3 months, 1 year, 3 years; 83% seen at 3 years), 1064 person-months; any use OR 5.3 (3.4-8.3); 1-15 days 4.0 (2.5-6.5); 16+ days 11.2 (5.9-21.1), all vs months of no methamphetamine use, adjusted for >=16 days of cannabis and/or alcohol use; further adjusted 2.25 (1.29-3.90) and 3.90 (1.80-8.45). Sample: MATES drew 400 people entering community treatment and 101 not in treatment (needle-syringe and outreach), so 'people with methamphetamine dependence' is accurate and 'in treatment' would not be. Exposure is self-reported days of use (Opiate Treatment Index), with hair-test confirmation of self-reported abstinence in 83 MATES participants (6% false reports).

anchors.extracted: 278 adults with DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence (CIDI), no lifetime schizophrenia or mania, from the MATES cohort (Sydney and Brisbane; 400 entering community treatment, 101 recruited through needle-syringe programmes and outreach). Interviews at baseline, 3 months, 1 year and 3 years (2006-2010); all seen at 3 and 12 months, 83% (230) at 3 years; 1064 months of data.

anchors.locator: Method > Measures; Design and statistical analysis
anchors.extracted: Outcome: BPRS score >=4 on suspiciousness, unusual thought content or hallucinations in the past month (interrater kappa 0.86). Exposure: days of methamphetamine use in past 4 weeks (Opiate Treatment Index); other drug days as time-varying covariates. Fixed-effects (within-person) logistic regression.

anchors.locator: Results > Relationship between psychotic symptoms and methamphetamine use; Table (model 2)
anchors.extracted: Model 2 (adjusted for >=16 days of cannabis and/or alcohol use): any use OR 5.3 (3.4-8.3); 1-15 days vs no use OR 4.0 (2.5-6.5); 16-28 days vs no use OR 11.2 (5.9-21.1). Unadjusted 4.8 (3.0-7.6) and 15.8 (8.6-28.7); model 1 (all drugs) 4.2 (2.5-7.3) and 12.0 (5.8-25.1). Frequent cannabis OR 2.0 (1.1-3.5) and alcohol 2.1 (1.1-4.2), relative to <16 days.

anchors.locator: Results, paragraph after the Table; Comment, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Predicted probability (model 2) with no methamphetamine use and <16 days of cannabis and alcohol use: 7%; with >=16 days of methamphetamine use: 48%; adding frequent cannabis and/or alcohol use: 61-69%.

Further adjustment for concurrent unemployment, unstable accommodation, low income, psychological distress and physical and mental disability: 1-15 days vs abstinence OR 2.25 (1.29-3.90), P=.004; 16+ days vs abstinence OR 3.90 (1.80-8.45), P<.001. Authors: these factors could not account for the relationship.

Mean age 31.7, 72% men, 78% unemployed; mean 13.1 years of use, 83% had injected; use in 58% of observed months (median 8 days in months of use; injecting the main route in 79%); tobacco, cannabis and alcohol common. Psychotic symptoms in 25% of months (273 of 1064); 60% of participants had symptoms in at least one observed month; mostly moderate (BPRS 4-5).
Authors: a clear dose-response, but chronicity of symptoms and longer-term vulnerability could not be determined; a small minority reported symptoms during abstinent periods.

key_findings.correction: 612 months with use recomputed from the Table (429 + 183); 612/1064 = 57.5%.

Estimates confirmed, but the note's 'roughly a halving' fits only the 1-15-day estimate (4.0 to 2.25, -44%); the 16+-day estimate fell by about two-thirds (11.2 to 3.90, -65%). Both retain about 56-58% of the log-odds. The same wording ('roughly halved the estimates') in the card's interpretation_gap, and in the claim, should be corrected.

NOT CHECKED rather than absent: Comment paragraphs 6-7 could not be read because the browser device disconnected after the Results and the start of the 5th Comment paragraph had been read. Not evidence that the statement is missing.

Partly checked: the 5th Comment paragraph's statement that a small minority reported symptoms during abstinent periods was read; the 'three readings' that follow were not reached (device disconnected).

reporting_issues.note: Not reported in the parts read (Methods, Results, Table).
Results: 'After adjusting for only those patterns of other drug use that showed evidence of an association'.
Consistent with the Methods (structured interview by trained interviewers rating BPRS and drug use); no blinding described.
Partly checked: header 'Published Online: March 2013' and '2013;70;(3):319-324' seen; the article-information date (9 January 2013) was not reached.

risk_of_bias.note: Substance agreed, labels not: 'moderate' is a ROBINS-I category (ROBINS-E: low / some concerns / high / very high), and with 'Selection of participants' rated high the ROBINS-E overall cannot be lower than high. In a within-person fixed-effects design, exclusion of non-attenders mainly limits generalizability rather than biasing the within-person contrast, so I would rate selection 'some concerns' and overall 'some concerns'; alternatively keep selection 'high' and make the overall 'high'.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor; correct 'roughly halved' for the 16+-day estimate (see key finding 8).

missed: Funding and conflict statements on the card (NHMRC grant 350974; disclosures) could not be re-checked by reader 2 because the article-information section was not reached before the browser device disconnected.

For cl_meth_psychosis_dose: the claim's 'roughly halved the odds ratios (2.25 and 3.90)' should read 'reduced them to 2.25 and 3.90' (16+ days: about a two-thirds reduction); the 7% and 48% predicted risks are conditional on fewer than 16 days of cannabis and alcohol use.

Arunogiri et al. (2018) describe this study's OR 11.2 as relative to fewer than 16 days of use; this paper's abstract and Table confirm the reference is months of no methamphetamine use (abstinence in the past month).
